analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from using bankruptcy to shield themselves from mass-tort lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 with three cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets a practice in which large companies facing thousands of injury lawsuits file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy not to reorganize, but to freeze the lawsuits and cap what they owe. It would let judges dismiss bankruptcy cases filed in bad faith, create a presumption of bad faith when a company manufactures a favorable court venue, and end the freeze (the automatic stay) that currently protects a company's parent companies and insurers from those lawsuits. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by products like talc, asbestos, or contaminated materials — the bill's definition covers claims involving 100 or more individuals — would keep their right to sue the parent companies, insurers, and affiliates that bankruptcy filings currently shield. General creditors would also gain, since bad-faith filings used to delay them could be dismissed.

how_it_helps.text: Judges could dismiss a Chapter 11 case that is 'objectively futile' or filed in subjective bad faith, closing the door on filings whose purpose is to dodge litigation rather than reorganize [S2].
A bankruptcy case is presumed filed in bad faith if the company manufactured the court venue, and the company can only rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence [S2].

The bankruptcy freeze on lawsuits would no longer automatically extend to a company's parents, insurers, and affiliates when the case follows a divisional merger or restructuring within the prior four years — the structure companies use to split liabilities away from assets before filing [S2].

A filing is conclusively presumed bad faith if its purpose is a tactical litigation advantage, delay of creditors, or capping liability to creditors holding mass-tort claims the company could pay in full [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability would bear the costs: they could no longer cap their exposure through bankruptcy, and they would face lawsuits against parent companies and insurers that are currently frozen. Their shareholders would absorb litigation costs and settlement payments.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies a conclusive presumption of bad faith, with the burden of proof on the debtor, whenever a company has undergone a divisional merger or restructuring in the prior four years — a rule that could dismiss legitimate reorganizations along with abusive ones [S2].

The 'protected claim' definition covers any claim affecting 100 or more people from a product or substance; companies argue that forcing tort suits to continue outside bankruptcy can produce slower, less coordinated compensation for victims than a structured bankruptcy settlement would [S2].
The amendments apply to cases already pending when the bill takes effect, which could upend reorganizations currently underway [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely criticized practice — companies splitting themselves apart, filing in a favorable venue, and using bankruptcy to cap their liability to injured people — and the people it protects are claimants and creditors with legitimate stakes. The trade-off is that its presumptions are unusually strict: a company that restructured for ordinary reasons and faces a genuine reorganizational path could still face dismissal or continued litigation. An honest assessment is that the bill is a strong corrective with a blunt edge; whether the blunt edge is acceptable depends on how much abuse of the venue-and-splitting strategy one believes is occurring.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on April 20, 2026, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the bill on April 20, 2026, joined by original cosponsors Rep. Gooden and Rep. Nadler [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, which is the last action of any kind in its record [S4].
The bill has three cosponsors total: one Republican and two Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the companies that use bankruptcy to cap mass-tort liability are better off: the current rules remain in place because the bill has not moved. Injury victims and creditors have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies still using bankruptcy to cap liability

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan from the start

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote in the record

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with two Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, and no floor vote exists to measure the parties against each other.

industries.industry: Large corporations facing mass-tort liability (talc, asbestos, opioid, contamination claims)
industries.note: The bill strips away the bankruptcy tools these companies use to freeze lawsuits, cap liability, and shield parents and insurers. Its central provisions are written around the 'protected claim' — a mass injury claim affecting 100 or more people — that drives the largest corporate bankruptcies.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate restructuring specialists
industries.note: The bill presumes bad faith when a filing follows a divisional merger or asset transfer to insiders within four years, directly targeting the split-the-company strategies that restructuring advisers design. Their clients lose a way to move liabilities away from assets before filing.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy law firms and venue advisors
industries.note: Cases can now be dismissed as futile or bad faith, and manufacturing the venue triggers a presumption of bad faith, shrinking the market for mega-Chapter 11 filings in favorable districts. Firms that steer these filings lose demand.

The bill lets injury suits proceed against nondebtor entities that provided insurance to the debtor, ending the automatic freeze insurers currently receive in these cases. They would face claims they can no longer defer through a debtor's bankruptcy.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one Republican cosponsor and no committee action since April 2026. Bills referred to the House Judiciary Committee rarely reach the floor without a chair-authorized markup or hearing, so unless leadership elevates it or support grows substantially, it is likely to die when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
